statement: In people who use benzodiazepines (prescribed, diverted, counterfeit or novel 'designer' benzodiazepines; most of the sources also involved opioids or stimulants), evidence is insufficient to say whether any harm reduction service or policy lowers harm. As described second-hand in a 2025 scoping review of 35 sources found up to July 2025, which mapped them without appraising them (Morrison et al., 2025), the approaches studied were drug checking (11 sources), prescribed benzodiazepines as treatment or safer supply (5), policies on scheduling, prescribing and surveillance (9) and approaches for particular groups (10); by the designs listed in the review's table, 17 were quantitative pilot, retrospective, cross-sectional or similar studies, 9 qualitative, 4 mixed-methods, 4 reviews and 1 a policy analysis, and none was a randomized trial. About half of the drug-checking sources (5 or 6 of 11 by the review's table, editors' count) tested how well drug-checking methods, mostly portable or point-of-care instruments checked against laboratory analysis, detect benzodiazepines: in 59 samples, a portable gas chromatography–mass spectrometer identified 36% of those containing etizolam (78% when etizolam was more than 3% of the sample by weight), against 9% with infrared spectroscopy. At one Canadian service, infrared analysis found alprazolam in 33 of 139 samples (23.7%) that people expected to be alprazolam (Xanax), and of 20 sent for confirmatory testing, 14 contained other active ingredients only. In a before-and-after pilot without a comparison group, among 68 of 103 women who do sex work and use drugs in Baltimore followed up a month after a fentanyl test-strip intervention, reported using alone fell from 96% to 68% and benzodiazepine use from 22% to 7%. In an observational study of 541 adults who use drugs in several US states, followed for 28 days, a positive fentanyl test-strip result went with reports of using smaller amounts, taking turns and keeping naloxone nearby, most strongly when benzodiazepines were tested; it relates test results to what people reported doing next, measures behaviour rather than harm and does not compare people offered drug checking with people who were not, and the review's text words this association as an effect. Prescribed benzodiazepines were described for 6 of 77 residents of COVID-19 isolation hotels, whose programme as a whole reported no overdoses (an evaluation the review cites as a preprint), and for more than 70 people experiencing homelessness in Dublin, from whom no feedback was collected; in one inner-London general practice, opioid substitution patients maintained on benzodiazepines (127 of 278) stayed in treatment longer than those prescribed none or only briefly (72 months against 34 and 51) and had a lower death rate in treatment than those prescribed none (1.31 against 1.79 per 100 patient-years; the review's table says the occasionally prescribed group had the lowest in-treatment death rate, without a figure), but a larger rise in deaths after leaving treatment, by figures the review reports inconsistently. After Australia moved alprazolam to a stricter schedule in 2014, four of five evaluations summarized in a 2021 review reported large falls in alprazolam use, along with falls in prescribing, dispensing, overdose deaths and poison-centre calls, while figures the authors cite from a letter, without definitions, show benzodiazepine overdose deaths overall rising from 160 in 2009 to 238 in 2015. After the United Kingdom rescheduled temazepam gel capsules, 100 people with long-term use of several drugs, in a qualitative study, described less injecting of capsules but continued injecting of tablets, higher prices, more acquisitive crime and substitution with flunitrazepam. The authors call drug checking the most widely reported approach, with consistently positive outcomes, and the results of prescribing and policy approaches mixed, without having appraised any source; they find harm reduction largely missing for people who are not seeking abstinence or treatment, and note that their search, built on the term harm reduction, may have missed studies. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Drug checking, prescribed benzos and stricter rules have all been tried for people who use benzos, but none has been tested in a way that shows whether it lowers harm. The review's authors call drug checking's results consistently positive, but those results are mostly about what tests detected and what people said they did afterwards. At one checking service, infrared testing found alprazolam, the drug in Xanax, in about 1 in 4 samples people thought were Xanax, and some testing methods often missed 'designer' benzos.
population: People who use benzodiazepines (prescribed, diverted, counterfeit or novel), in 35 sources gathered by one scoping review, most of which also involved opioids or stimulants: drug samples at checking services, clients of harm reduction services, women who do sex work, residents of COVID-19 isolation hotels, people in treatment, emergency-department and festival patients, forum posters and poison-centre callers
exposure: Harm reduction services and policies: drug checking, prescribed benzodiazepines (agonist treatment or safer supply), rescheduling, prescribing rules, toxicosurveillance and a poison-centre line
comparator: Mostly none; a few observational comparisons (patients maintained on benzodiazepines against others; positive against negative test results), before-and-after measurements without a control group, and one detection method against another (mostly portable or point-of-care methods against laboratory analysis)
outcome: Detection of benzodiazepines in drug samples; reported behaviour after testing; treatment retention and mortality; prescribing, use and deaths after policy changes; people's accounts
magnitude: No pooled estimates. Detection: portable gas chromatography–mass spectrometry 36% of etizolam-containing samples (78% above 3% by weight) against 9% with infrared (59 samples); a miniature mass spectrometer quantified etizolam in 11 of 15 samples that strips and/or infrared had failed to detect or quantify. Expected alprazolam: 33 of 139 (23.7%) by infrared; of 20 confirmed, 2 alprazolam alone, 4 alprazolam with other ingredients, 14 other ingredients only. Toronto: of 555 samples, 15 were expected to be benzodiazepines, and benzodiazepine-type drugs were found in 116; benzodiazepine-type drugs present in 24 (41%) of samples linked to a negative effect (presence, not cause). After test strips (pilot, 68 of 103 followed up): using alone 96% to 68%, benzodiazepine use 22% to 7%; 69% reported a harm reduction behaviour. Test-strip results and later behaviour (541 adults, 28 days, observational): a positive result went with using smaller amounts, taking turns and keeping naloxone nearby, most strongly when benzodiazepines were tested (sizes given only in the review's table, second-hand, without a description of the measure). Prescribed benzodiazepines: 6 of 77 hotel residents (cited from a preprint); more than 70 people in Dublin. Opioid substitution case notes: retention 72 against 34 and 51 months; in-treatment mortality 1.31 against 1.79 per 100 patient-years (against those prescribed none; lowest in the occasionally prescribed group, no figure given); post-treatment rate in the maintained group 5.90 per 100 years, reported as a 450% rise (4.5 times the in-treatment rate, an increase of about 350%, editors' calculation). Alprazolam rescheduling: 4 of 5 evaluations reported large declines in use; alprazolam-related deaths 57 (2012) to 23 (2015); benzodiazepine overdose deaths 160 (2009) to 238 (2015). Kentucky 'no benzodiazepine' formulary: prescriptions down 89% over two years. Victoria emergency departments, 2020 to 2022: novel benzodiazepine-type drugs in 183 of 1112 drug-toxicity presentations (16.5%). Poison-centre line: safety information to 6635 of 17,616 callers (37.7%), no outcome evaluation.

risk_of_bias.note: No included source was appraised; designs are pilot, cross-sectional, qualitative, uncontrolled before-and-after or descriptive; the review attributes programme-wide outcomes to benzodiazepine prescribing, and its counts contain errors (card sc_morrison_2025); the isolation-hotel evaluation is cited from a preprint.

inconsistency.note: Not rated: different approaches, not repeated tests of one approach.

indirectness.note: Second-hand, and some figures third-hand (a 2021 review and a letter cited by the authors); detection accuracy stands in for outcomes that matter to people; most people and samples involved opioids and other drugs as well.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed; grey and peer-led literature were not searched.

grade.reasoning: Observational and descriptive sources start low; rated down for risk of bias and indirectness, giving very low. The claim rests only on a scoping review, a narrative synthesis without appraisal (designed as a narrative review on its card), so it stays at draft and its figures are second-hand (METHODS §6.3). Insufficient evidence: no approach was evaluated against a comparison able to show an effect on harm; the only comparisons are observational (one practice's case notes; test-strip results related to later reported behaviour, an outcome of behaviour, not harm) or before-and-after without a control group, and the authors' more favourable reading of drug checking rests on detection studies and reported behaviour. Status single study: the claim rests on one review, and no approach has two controlled evaluations. The primary sources (for example the alprazolam test results, the test-strip pilot and the London case notes) have not been read.
